new_statements.quote: In English, every word must have a primary stress whereas in Ikom language such a rule does not exist. This accounts for the deviations in the use of English primary stress pattern noticed among the students (Ikom learners of English). The chief reason for this deviation is that, English is an international (stress timed) language while Ikom language is a tonal (syllable-timed) language.

new_statements.relation_note: An English-interference study by non-specialists, not a description: in its literature review (p. 42) 'English is an intonational (stress timed) language while Nigerian indigenous languages are tonal (syllable timed) languages of which Ikom language is not an exception'; in the discussion of the primary-stress test (p. 51) it states that Ikom has no rule assigning a primary word stress and is 'a tonal (syllable-timed) language'; p. 52 'none of the students were able to place primary stress correctly, owing to the fact that English is international [sic, = intonational] while Ikom is tonal.. every syllable in certain words were stressed by the students'; findings p. 54 repeat 'all Nigerian l…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ikom is characterised as a tone (syllable-timed) language with no word-level primary stress rule; nothing on the number of tones or their behaviour.
new_statements.identity_note: A's WORK 3 (pointer, abstract only), added: open copy downloaded from the the Internet Archive (publisher host could not be reached by automated download) and a stress/tone statement A could not see. The L1 is 'Ikom language', the native language of 120 SS3 students at Government Secondary School Ikom, Holy Child Secondary School Ikom and St. Patrick's Secondary School Ikom (Ikom town, Ikom LGA, Cross River State). The paper gives no genetic classification, ISO code or alternative name; the language called 'Ikom' in Ikom town is the Ikom (Nkome) variety of Olulumo-Ikom (olul1245); the other L1s of the LGA go by their own names (Yala, Bakor/Nde, Ejagham), so attribution to olul1245 (Ikom variety, not Olulumo/Okuni) is probable but not proven. Segmental claims made in passing (no /p/-/b/ contrast, [g] an allophone of /k/, no /v/, no schwa) could be checked against the Nkome Luke orthography by a later reading.

sources.citation: Luke Initiative for Scripture Translation. 2024. Olulumo-Ikom Bible [Gospel of Luke; YouVersion version id 3993, abbreviation OLULUMO-IKOM, (c) 2024 Luke Initiative for Scripture Translation]. Online text. (A second Luke translation for iko, distinct from the 2022 'Nkome LP NT Portions', version 3430.)
sources.note: Nothing: scripture text with no orthography note. The practical orthography (ɔ ɛ ɨ ŋ, ch ny kp gb) carries no tone or accent diacritics in either chapter read, so it yields neither a statement nor tone-marked data. It does show that LIST ran two Luke projects (Nkome 2022, Olulumo-Ikom 2024), so two project-internal orthography statements presumably exist offline.

sources.citation: Luke Initiative for Scripture Translation / The Seed Company. 2022. Nkome LP NT Portions [Gospel of Luke in Nkome (Olulumo-Ikom, iko)]. Online text, YouVersion version id 3430 (©2022 Luke Initiative for Scripture Translation); listed by find.bible as 'Nkome Luke, Olulumo-Ikom, 2022' (IKOCAB).
sources.note: Scripture text only, no orthography statement. The practical orthography uses ɛ, ɔ, ɨ, ŋ and digraphs (ny, kp, gb) and carries NO tone or accent diacritics (e.g. 'Kegbu kanci, Ɔkɨm Ɛmaŋ Ɔgɔstus ɔjɛ nsɨm ya oni naŋɔnɛ..'), so it yields neither a statement nor marked prosodic data. An orthography guide presumably exists within the LIST/Seed Company project but is not online.

sources.citation: [Authorship not stated in the file; hosted on Victor Manfredi's Boston University page and, on internal evidence ('p.c. to I. Miller', Cabrera's Abakuá word list), the etymological appendix prepared with Ivor L. Miller for the 2020 English edition of Lydia Cabrera's La lengua sagrada de los ñáñigos.] c. 2020. Appendix: Cross River etymologies. 27 pp. PDF (created 2 July 2020).
sources.note: Wordlist-level datum only: one Olulumo-Ikom lexeme, tone-marked Low-Low, in the etymology of Abakuá maya 'river' ('< Òlúlùmọ́-Íkóm màyà "river", cf. Èkóí àyà (Okongor 1982, 5, 75, Roseline Égbè p.c.)'). The introduction states the editors' general convention ('We attempt full tonemarking: each high syllable has an acute accent, each low syllable has a grave accent and a syllable with no mark has unknown pitch'), applying to all cited languages; there is no statement about the tone system, accent or stress of Olulumo-Ikom itself. The glossonym is itself fully tone-marked.

sources.citation: Johnston, Harry H. 1922. A comparative study of the Bantu and Semi-Bantu languages. Vol. II. Oxford: Clarendon Press. [Remarks on no. 238 Olulɔmɔ and 238a Ikom in the chapters on prefixes/concords and pronouns, pp. 234-235 and passim in the root analyses.]
sources.note: Nothing on prosody. Content is comparative morphology: loss of initial M- in class 1 prefix, Ke-/Bi- (7/8), Ja-, En-, Ma-, Je-, Da-/Ra- plural prefixes, diminutive Won- 'child', 2pl pronoun Wun, plus scattered lexical root comparisons citing 238. The phonology chapters do not single out 238/238a.

sources.note: No phonology content: numerals, c. 45 nouns with class prefixes segmented (Ko-bɔ 'arm', Ke-tet 'beard', De-yu 'belly'..), an inventory of singular/plural prefixes matched to Bantu classes, and a location note. No tone or stress marks and no remark on accent or tone for 238/238a.
